pandas.q: In pandas, what is a DataFrame?
options: A single column of values with one data type
A table of rows and named columns, each column with its own type
A chart drawn from a CSV file
A connection to a SQL database
pandas.why: A DataFrame is the whole table. A single column is a Series.

pandas.q: You load a CSV and the amount column shows dtype str (or object). What does that most likely mean?
options: pandas always loads numbers as text
The file is too large to parse
At least one value is not a clean number, such as "1,250.00"
The column has no missing values
pandas.why: One non-numeric value makes pandas keep the whole column as text. Find and fix those values, then convert with pd.to_numeric.

pandas.q: A UK customer's export has dates like 03/04/2026. What should you do before parsing?
options: Let pandas guess the format automatically
Confirm it is day first, then parse with format="%d/%m/%Y"
Drop the date column since it is ambiguous
Parse with the US format because it is the default
pandas.why: 03/04 is 3 April day-first and 4 March month-first. Ask, then give an explicit format so every row is read the same way.

pandas.q: After merging orders with a customer lookup, your row count goes from 10,000 to 10,240 and revenue rises. What is the likely cause?
options: Some customer IDs appear more than once in the lookup
The merge used how="left"
Some orders had missing amounts
The orders file was sorted differently
pandas.why: Duplicate keys on the right side copy matching left rows: fan-out. Use validate="many_to_one" and fix the lookup.

pandas.q: A teammate fills every missing amount with 0 so the totals look complete. What is the problem?
options: fillna does not work on numeric columns
It makes the file larger
pandas cannot sum a column that was filled
It changes sums and averages and hides that data is missing
pandas.why: A blank is not a zero unless the customer says so. Flag missing values and report them instead of guessing.

debugging.q: How should you read a Python traceback?
options: Top down, the first line shows the error
Bottom up, the last line shows the exception and message
Only the middle frames matter
Ignore it and add print statements
debugging.why: The bottom line gives the exception type and message, and the frame above shows where it broke. Then walk up to the first frame in your own code.

Merges two branches halfway
Binary-searches commit history to find the first bad commit
Reverts the last half of your commits
debugging.why: You mark a good and a bad commit and git halves the range each test. With a repro script, git bisect run automates it.

debugging.q: A customer's nightly job failed in a repo you have never seen. What is your first step?
options: Get the logs and input of the failed run and reproduce it
Rewrite the job in a style you know better
Add retries around every external call
Upgrade all dependencies to their latest versions
debugging.why: Reproducing with the real input gives you a test for every later step. Rewrites and upgrades change many things before you know the cause.

debugging.q: A log shows 300 errors from last night's run. Which one do you look at first?
options: The last error, since it is the most recent
The most frequent error message
A random sample of ten errors
The first error around the time things went wrong
debugging.why: Later errors are often consequences of the first failure. Fixing the first one frequently removes all the others.

debugging.q: A sync job loses a few records with no error, and someone wraps it in try/except and adds retries. What is the mistake?
options: try/except is slower than if statements
It hides the cause, and retries cannot fix code that thinks it succeeded
Retries should only be added in tests
Exceptions must always be re-raised twice
debugging.why: Nothing was failing, so retries change nothing and broad excepts hide future errors. Reproduce, find the cause, fix it with a test.
